title: Privacy by design
summary: The safest data to protect is data the service never receives.

steps.title: A wearable knows more than the dashboard needs
steps.text: A wrist device samples motion every second. The person wants a daily activity summary, not a server-side copy of every movement. Uploading all raw readings creates a sensitive archive and an ongoing deletion obligation. Start by asking which feature needs which data, who can read it and how long it must exist.

steps.title: Move the boundary deliberately
steps.text: Choose where each field is readable. Device-only data cannot power a server feature; end-to-end encrypted payloads still reveal upload metadata. Inspect the breach boundary.

steps.title: Worked example: sparse uploads
steps.text: Less payload reduces the sensitive archive, but a daily summary can still reveal health information. Consent, authorization and retention remain necessary. These decimal byte calculations do not measure radio energy. A passing traffic day cannot prove device isolation, encryption or legal compliance.

diagram.label: Collect only the feature payload
parts: 16 bytes × 86,400 samples. About 41.5 MB for 30 days.
About 690 times less payload, still sensitive information.
Consent, authorization and deletion apply to summaries too.

steps.q: The service itself decrypts uploaded notes to build an ordinary search index. Which privacy claim is accurate?
choices: Content is encrypted in transit and storage, but readable by the service
Content is end-to-end encrypted because only the indexing worker has the key
Content is hidden from the service if the worker discards plaintext after indexing
steps.why: Temporary or restricted server access is still plaintext access within the service trust boundary.

steps.q: Can we keep server search and claim the service cannot read notes? Follow-up: what does the first version offer?
checklist: Keep note keys and plaintext search indexes on authorized devices
Name timing and size leakage and the loss of ordinary server search
Describe authenticated enrollment and a user-held recovery secret
steps.model: Ordinary server plaintext indexing contradicts that claim. In the first version, devices encrypt notes with a random collection key and search a local plaintext index. An existing authorized device authenticates enrollment and wraps the collection key for the new device. A user-held recovery secret can unwrap a separately stored encrypted key backup; the server never receives that secret. Losing every device and the recovery secret means losing access. Timing and sizes still leak metadata. If server plaintext processing is required, I would change the trust claim explicitly.

steps.title: Keys and deletion are workflows
steps.text: Use authenticated encryption, unique nonces and well-reviewed libraries. Protect data keys with wrapping keys in a device key store. Routine rotation can rewrap keys; a compromised wrapping key may already have exposed them, requiring new data keys for future content. Revocation cannot recall copied plaintext. Deletion must cover object versions, exports and backups as well as live rows. Cryptographic erasure requires every usable copy of the relevant key to be gone.

diagram.label: Deletion needs a receipt
parts: Retire device access and rotate affected keys. Already copied plaintext cannot be recalled.
Delete rows, versions, indexes, caches and exports; track backup expiry.
Check that a restored backup reapplies deletion receipts before serving data.

steps.q: Every authorized device is lost. The service holds no content recovery secret. What could still restore encrypted notes?
choices: A password reset plus a fresh device-generated content key
A recovery secret the user saved before the loss
Rewrapping the stored ciphertext with a new server metadata key
steps.why: A new key cannot decrypt old ciphertext. Recovery needs an existing content key or a secret that can unwrap it.

steps.q: The customer asks for proof of deletion. What can we actually prove? Follow-up: a backup is restored next week.
checklist: Inventory object versions, indexes, backups and usable key copies
State per-store deletion evidence and backup expiry deadlines
Reapply the deletion ledger before a restored backup serves requests
steps.model: I can provide evidence that our managed stores processed a deletion, with per-store receipts, object-version checks and key-lifecycle records. I cannot prove an endpoint never copied plaintext. Restores must reapply a deletion ledger before serving data, or the backup must already be unreadable through complete key erasure. I would state when backups expire and test a restore against that promise. Keeping the evidence minimal avoids creating a new archive of the deleted content.

steps.q: Active rows are deleted, but retained backups still contain decryptable copies. Which receipt is accurate?
choices: Deletion is complete because backups are not part of the live service
Deletion is complete once the current wrapping key is rotated
Active deletion is verified; backup expiry and restore suppression remain tracked
steps.why: Retained keys may still decrypt backups after rotation. Receipts must state the remaining backup boundary and deadline.

takeaway: Choose what leaves the device, who holds keys and how deletion finishes before collecting data.
